analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the federal watchdog for loans, credit cards, and debt collection.
analysis.headline: The bill to eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau was introduced in February 2017 with 31 Republican cosponsors and died in the House Financial Services Committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill repeals the 2010 law that created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). The CFPB is the agency that writes and enforces rules on mortgages, credit cards, payday loans, student loan servicing, and debt collection, and that returns money to consumers who were cheated. Eliminating it would leave consumer protection in these markets to scattered, weaker regulators. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Lenders and financial firms that faced CFPB enforcement: payday lenders, debt collectors, credit card issuers, and mortgage companies. Eliminating the bureau would remove the agency that sues them, caps certain fees, and forces refunds to customers who were overcharged or deceived.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010 in its entirety, which would abolish the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and restore the pre-2010 legal landscape in consumer finance.
Firms subject to CFPB rules on credit cards, mortgages, payday loans, and debt collection would no longer face a dedicated regulator with power to investigate, fine, and order refunds.

The repeal includes a provision restoring or reviving the provisions of law as they stood before the 2010 act, meaning the agency and its rulemaking and enforcement authorities would be erased rather than merely renamed.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers of financial products. Without the CFPB, households borrowing for a home, carrying credit card debt, or dealing with debt collectors would have fewer protections and no single agency to complain to when they are charged illegal fees or misled about loan terms.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the bureau point to its record of returning billions of dollars to consumers and policing payday lenders and debt collectors; repealing the law would eliminate that enforcement entirely, leaving wronged borrowers to sue on their own.

Supporters of repeal argued the CFPB is unaccountable: it is funded directly from the Federal Reserve rather than through the congressional appropriations process, and its director had broad unilateral power, which critics said let one unelected official rewrite credit markets without oversight. Repealing the whole act, rather than reforming its structure, was the bluntest available answer to that complaint.

Consumers with no formal education in finance bear the burden of displacement: complex credit contracts and aggressive collection practices are precisely the areas where individual borrowers have the least ability to protect themselves without an agency enforcer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers no replacement protections; it is a straight elimination of the one agency dedicated to policing consumer credit. The genuine concern about the bureau's structure and funding could be addressed by narrower reform, but this bill chose total repeal. The cost would fall on households least equipped to police lenders themselves, while the gain would accrue to firms the bureau fines and sues.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it never reached the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. John Ratcliffe (R-TX) introduced the bill on February 14, 2017, with 13 original cosponsors, all Republicans.
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day, the only committee action in the record.
It drew 30 Republican cosponsors in total and no Democrats, and received no further action: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, for the remainder of the 115th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with the bill still in committee, so it never came to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers kept the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and its enforcement powers, because the bill never advanced. Banks, payday lenders, and debt collectors did not get the repeal they sought, and the bill's backers made no progress toward it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers; the bureau survived the Congress

for.name: Rep. John Ratcliffe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the 2010 law creating the CFPB.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and no vote was ever taken to test broader support.

industries.note: The CFPB wrote rules restricting payday and auto-title loans and sued lenders for trapping borrowers in debt cycles. Repeal would have removed its most active adversary; the industry's gain would have come directly from borrowers paying higher-cost loans.

Debt collection is one of the CFPB's largest complaint categories, and the bureau fines collectors for illegal practices. Abolishing it would have left consumers with no federal complaint desk for collection abuse.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer banks
industries.note: The bureau caps certain fees, polices card disclosures, and orders refunds for overcharges. Repeal would have freed issuers from the agency that returns money to their customers.
The CFPB enforces mortgage disclosure and servicing rules created after the 2008 crisis and handles foreclosure-related enforcement. Its elimination would have removed the main cop on those rules.
